title: “Postmodernism:”
summary: Josh and Chuck explore postmodernism as a broad cultural worldview rather than just an art movement. They cover its roots in reaction to modernism and the horrors of world wars, science and reason; the idea of rejecting universal truth and meta-narratives (Nietzsche, Jean-François Lyotard's 1979 definition); Marcel Duchamp's readymades such as Fountain; postmodern art (Magritte's The Treachery of Images, Joseph Kosuth's One and Three Chairs, Piss Christ and the NEA funding controversy); postmodern literature (Calvino's If on a Winter's Night a Traveler, Pynchon, Heller, Vonnegut); film (Fellini's 8½, Pulp Fiction, Charlie Kaufman, Tarantino pastiche, intertextuality via John Munch); postmodern architecture (Frank Gehry, Guggenheim buildings); criticisms from left and right and the link to late capitalism; and what comes next (hypermodernism, metamodernism, Sturgill Simpson's album Metamodern Sounds in Country Music). The episode ends with listener mail about sinusitis causing toothache.

segments.title: Opening and defining postmodernism
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the difficulty of defining postmodernism as an era and a worldview shared culturally, not just an art movement, and note its fuzzy boundaries.

segments.title: Rejecting universal truth and modernism
segments.summary: Postmodernism is described as rejecting universal truth and meta-narratives, breaking from modernism's faith in reason; Nietzsche's perspectivism is discussed as an early influence, along with the reaction to World War I, World War II and the nuclear bomb.

segments.title: Lyotard's definition and metanarratives
segments.summary: Jean-François Lyotard coined the term in 1979, defining postmodernism as incredulity toward metanarratives; the hosts discuss skepticism, irony and sarcasm as hallmarks.

segments.title: Duchamp and postmodern art
segments.summary: Marcel Duchamp's readymades, especially Fountain (1917), are presented as an early postmodern gesture that blurred high and low art; the hosts connect this to Warhol, consumerism and art as advertising.

segments.title: Magritte, Kosuth and the Piss Christ controversy
segments.summary: Magritte's The Treachery of Images and Joseph Kosuth's One and Three Chairs illustrate questioning representation; the hosts recount the late-1980s Piss Christ controversy and NEA funding cuts.

segments.title: Postmodern literature
segments.summary: Postmodern novelists such as Pynchon and Heller pushed fragmentation and paradox, with Calvino's If on a Winter's Night a Traveler as an example; the hosts discuss criticism that meaning is empty.

segments.title: Postmodern film and intertextuality
segments.summary: Films such as Fellini's 8½, Pulp Fiction, and Charlie Kaufman's work are discussed as postmodern; intertextuality (John Munch across TV shows) and pastiche (Tarantino, Wes Anderson) are explained.

segments.title: Postmodern architecture and Guggenheims
segments.summary: Frank Gehry is presented as a postmodern starchitect, contrasted with Frank Lloyd Wright's Guggenheim in New York and Gehry's Guggenheim in Spain; the hosts discuss the New York museum.

segments.title: Criticisms, late capitalism, and what comes next
segments.summary: Criticisms of postmodernism from left and right are discussed, linking it to neoliberal economics and late capitalism; successors hypermodernism and metamodernism are described, with Sturgill Simpson's album as an example.

segments.title: Listener mail: nose breathing and toothache
segments.summary: A listener, dentist Tom Park, explains that sinusitis can cause toothache-like pain because maxillary sinuses sit near the roots of upper teeth; Josh shares his own sinus lift story.
